constructions.support: wǣron fullfręmede = were completed/finished; the coordinated subject is the heavens, the earth, and all their array. wǣron is a familiar form but this use with a participle remains supplied.
Eornostlice = accordingly/thus; ðā = then, an adverb rather than the identically spelled article. No article form is being parsed at those tokens.
eall hiera frætwung = all their array; eall modifies feminine singular frætwung. fram eallum ðǣm weorce = from all the work; eallum and ðǣm agree with neuter dative singular weorce.
ðone seofoðan dæg = the seventh day: masculine accusative singular with the actual weak ordinal form seofoðan. No other ordinal forms are required.

on ðone seofoðan dæg = on the seventh day; on ðone dæg = on that day/the day just named. These are temporal phrases with accusative. Do not replace dæg with dative dæge or infer motion. Unit 1 locative on + dative does not license this use.

ðe introduces which/that clauses referring to work: which he made; which he performed; which he created to make. The relative particle represents the direct object within each clause, although its antecedents weorc, weorce, weorces have different external cases. Supply clause boundaries and this relation; do not assign general relative syntax.

Each of the six verbs is third-person singular preterite indicative. Their finite paradigms/senses must be taught before the reading; local support must not substitute for those missing prerequisites.
hiera is a plural possessor of array; his is masculine singular possessor of work. These genitive pronouns are indeclinable possessors and do not agree with the possessed noun's case.
hē geręste hine uses ordinary accusative hine reflexively. The later hine is an ordinary object whose masculine antecedent is dæg. Pronoun reference depends on the sentence, not the spelling alone.

Here geręstan + reflexive pronoun + fram-phrase means rest from work. fram governs dative weorce. The form of fram and separation use were taught in Unit 1, but that contract confined independent use to a supplied separating frame.
for-ðon-ðe introduces the reason: because he ceased from his work on that day. The clause continues through the final supplied relative/infinitive phrase.

geswāc his weorces = ceased from his work. geswāc governs genitive weorces; his is its possessive genitive, not a second direct object. The known genitive form does not imply this new government was taught.

ðe hē gescēop tō wyrceanne = which he created to make. Cook gives Latin creavit ut faceret and the margin rendering created to make. tō wyrceanne is an inflected infinitive indicating the making for which he created the work. Preserve the actual source relation; do not silently substitute created and made or finished creating. This compact calque is supplied whole, with no independent infinitive target or unique idiomatic-translation demand.

audited_inflection_rules.statement: Attributive and ordinary predicative adjectives agree in gender, number and case with their noun/referent; predicate positive adjectives are strong.
Ordinary adjective after demonstrative/article is weak; comparative always weak; ordinal weak except ōðer; superlative normally weak attributively and strong in the taught predicate use.

The six selected possessives decline strongly and agree with the possessed noun, not the owner. A following ordinary adjective may be strong or weak: Cook says sometimes weak; avoid imposing one universal choice.
Bounded A + copula + comparative + ðonne + B: when A and B are the contrasted subjects, B is nominative and the repeated copula may remain unexpressed. This does not cover every comparative clause.

Distinct strong adjective/demonstrative M/N singular instrumental forms are reference recognition only; agreement, manner, means, comparison-measure and prepositional instrumental syntax are not assigned. Weak instrumental shares dative forms, not an additional taught construction.

One modifies singular count nouns; two/three inflect for plural noun gender/case. Four through twelve are taught in ordinary uninflected pre-nominal use with plural count nouns and plural verb agreement. Plural ān is reference-only, weak āna alone unassigned.
Selected adjective bases yield -e or -lice adverbs; regular degree -or/-ost, with wel/bęt/bętst memorized separately. Adverbs are indeclinable and can qualify verbs/adjectives/other adverbs.

Use the selected lemma rows, not a universal instruction to delete medial vowels. Long disyllables often shorten before vowel endings but retain the medial vowel before consonantal -ne/-re/-ra; analogical and endingless-u alternatives are lexical/pattern choices.

independent_source_translation.text: God then said, “Let there now be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them separate day and night, and let them be for signs, for seasons, for days, and for years. And let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth”; it then came to pass thus. And God made two great lights: the greater light for the illumination of the day, and the lesser light for the illumination of the night; and he made stars. And he set them in heaven, so that they might shine over the earth, rule over the day and the night, and separate light and darkness; God then saw that it was good. And evening and morning came to pass, the fourth day.
notes: sōðlice is a narrative connective here (source note15: Latin autem), not a compulsory emphatic claim “truly”. The English opening absorbs this connective.
“Let there be” renders a finite plural wish, not an infinitive. Each coordinated optative belongs to the wish or later purpose construction.
“Be for signs/seasons...” can idiomatically become “serve as signs...” but that is an English paraphrase, not an extra Old English verb.
The paired greater and lesser lights are unnamed in this source span. Do not replace them in the transcript or translation with sun and moon.
The closing source order and resultative formula are kept distinct from the simpler independent copula system. An idiomatic “there came evening and morning, the fourth day” preserves the sequence.
The final clauses say that the lights rule over day/night and divide light/darkness. They do not merely restate illumination.

new_sense_distinction.weorthan-become: ordinary become with explicitly taught nominative predicate

audited_inflection_rules.text: Use four principal parts. Present 1sg/pl use the present stem; present 2/3sg have the audited mutation/consonant changes. Past1/3sg normally share the singular stem; past2sg uses the plural stem plus -e, and all plural persons use -on. findan requires the separately printed exception.
Infinitive and past participle are citation/reference support only. No new perfect, passive, infinitive clause, participial agreement or prefix rule follows from a principal-parts table.
Class I normally ī : ā : i : i. Snīðan changes ð to d in plural-based past forms and participle. Contracted wrēon has a special present and h/g stems.
Class II normally ēo or ū : ēa : u : o. Present2/3sg ēo→īe and ū→ȳ; Cook also allows ī for īe. cēosan s/r, sēoðan ð/d, and tēon h/g are lexical changes.

III has several present/past-singular families, not one interchangeable vowel formula: bindan i/a/u/u, helpan e/ea/u/o, gieldan ie/ea/u/o, weorpan eo/ea/u/o, berstan e/æ/u/o. All those selected vowels are short. weorðan adds ð/d; winnan reduces nn; findan, bregdan and fēolan need explicit exception notes.

Dental d/t+ð gives tt (or t); d+st gives tst. s+st/ð gives st; ð before st may disappear and ð+ð may reduce. Geminates reduce before consonantal endings. g/h alternatives require the stated long-vowel/liquid environment; do not substitute h indiscriminately.

Cook permits full -est/-eð forms as well as syncopated cells. Their vowel can preserve an older mutated stem or be restored analogically; the audit selects complete contracted rows and records specifically checked variants rather than generating every possible full-ending spelling. A correct documented variant is not wrong merely for differing from the recall target.

Recognize present plural -e before an immediately following subject pronoun (Cook binde wē). This is conditioned by word order and is not a global alternative to -að after a preceding subject; production tasks may retain subject-before-verb.

Tōberstan and forweorðan are independently sourced lexemes, then expanded by identified base morphology. Their meanings and intransitive source frames are separate. No arbitrary prefix attachment or sense composition is licensed.
Extend prior preverbal ne to the introduced noncontracting strong indicatives. Keep negative copula, nillan and other contracted systems outside this extension.
Ordinary weorðan become can take a nominative predicate adjective agreeing with the subject. The finite indicative system does not promote old supplied passive constructions.

The finite paradigm does not establish object case. In particular helpan permits genitive or dative (selected dative here); bēodan command, gieldan repayment, bregdan instrumental use and other complements require separate teaching. Morphology-only verbs may be practised with person/tense labels without composing an unsupported clause.

audited_inflection_rules.text: Present1sg -e and plural -að use the present stem; present2/3 require the selected mutation/consonant rules. Preterite1/3sg share the singular stem; preterite2sg uses the plural stem plus -e; all plural persons use -on. Contracted and j-present rows are explicit.

Use complete singular/plural imperative pairs for selected lexical models covering weak I–III, strong I–VII and needed anomalous patterns, including important exceptions and simple negative commands.
Use the selected plain/inflected infinitive pairs in elementary modal/volitional complements and bounded purposive cuman+tō constructions, retaining each lexical government.
Distinguish knowledge of a matter from learned ability, modal sense from morphological tense, and volition from completed action; use new and prior material in meaningful connected practice.
Complete all72 original graded tasks, read the checked controlled dialogue independently, and interpret the exact fisherman excerpt with its explicitly bounded support.
recognition_outcomes: Distinguish actual usable forms from uncertain or unattested modal citation labels; no regular modal imperative or inflected infinitive is invented.
Distinguish taught infinitive morphology from supplied availability, relative, content and participial constructions in the source.
Distinguish selected course forms from valid documented alternatives and unassigned additional lexical rows.
bounded_scope: First/second personal genitives remain recognition-only; agreeing possessives are separate productive lemmas.
Instrumental forms, plural ān and eall remain recognition/reference; *sǣwa remains a supplied starred reconstruction without milestones.
Nabban, bregdan and fēolan remain at prior recognition scope; their presence in a prior table does not authorize productive new commands.
Diagnostic īecan, gierwan, ęfnan and hycgan lack arbitrary productive argument frames; use isolated form exercises unless a frame is expressly audited.
Hātan active indicative morphology does not teach hātte, infinitival causatives or double-accusative naming.
Beodan offer and lǣtan let do not automatically license command/causative complement frames; biddan ask needs an explicit new construction if used with an infinitive.
Prior source-only temporal/connective ðā, nū, ęft, swā, sōðlice, destination tō, motion on, mid and relative/content/purpose clauses remain supplied unless explicitly newly taught.
Simple ne negation extends only to newly audited systems; no negative copula, negative concord or every contracted negative form follows.
Participles, passive, subjunctive/optative wishes and unsupported subordinate moods remain supplied/deferred. Creation wishes must not be labelled imperative morphology.
No ge- or other prefix generalization; new prefixed lexemes need their own evidence.
I.4.18 and the birds candidate remain Unit7 deferrals; no earlier active or archived artifact is rewritten.
Only43 imperative-model lemma systems (44 rows with alternate bēon) and two additional infinitive-only skill verbs receive these new nonfinite/imperative milestones.

grammar_audit_boundaries.claim: Infinitive-looking headwords are unattested citation labels, supported by Fulk§123 and partly flagged by Cook125. No inflected infinitive or imperative generated.
No positive imperative assigned. Cook139 supplies only negative plural nellað/nyllað; do not invent singular will or pair will/willað.

Cook §126/§198 and Wright §540 call wite (and Wright witaþ) imperative. Fulk §123 says preterite-presents have no formal imperative and use subjunctive substitutes. No regular modal imperative system is generated or assigned here; documented command substitutes are not denied.

grammar_audit_boundaries.claim: No imperative in Cook130–131 or Fulk123; no complete imperative pair proposed. Attested uninflected citations do not license unattested modal imperative reconstruction.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Selected preterite-presents have present 1sg=3sg, a special 2sg, and one plural stem/form for all persons; their past is weak. Learn each selected present/past pair as a complete indicative system.
Where Cook prints the past in -e followed by etc., the 2sg adds -st and the plural changes -e to -on. These are declared model-derived cells, not separately quoted textual tokens.
Don, gan, and willan have complete selected present/preterite indicative systems. Gan uses eode for the past; willan has wille in both present 1sg and 3sg, not an automatically added ordinary -ð.
The six beo/bist/bið/beoð indicative person cells supplement the prior wesan system and share its prior past; future or habitual/gnomic state depends on context.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Productive use is explicitly contextualized expected-later state; no new tense of every verb or future auxiliary willan is inferred.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Second singular commands address one person; second plural commands address more than one. The subject may be omitted or stated.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Only selected second-person systems are assigned. First/third-person optative commands remain later scope.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Ordinary strong singular imperative is the present stem without the infinitive ending; the second plural normally matches the present indicative plural. Present 2sg/3sg mutation is not mechanically imported into the command stem.

Contracted strong verbs restore final h in the singular command: wrīh, tēoh, seoh, sleah, fōh. The vowel qualities/quantities are lexical class patterns; seoh/sleah are short, wrīh/tēoh/fōh retain the selected long vowel. Their plurals remain contracted.

Heavy weak-I singular commands lack final -e; short/geminate-j patterns retain -e and lose the j-induced gemination in the singular: nęre/nęriað, fręme/fręmmað, sęle/sęllað, sęte/sęttað. Gierwan has giere/gierwað.
Selected heavy weak-I cys and gefyl simplify the final double consonant; plurals cyssað and gefyllað retain it. This is distinct from the short-stem -e model and from settan, whose singular is sete.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Final simplification is frequent and the selected normalized model; do not assert that all unsimplified final spellings are impossible.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Strong j-presents use weak-I-like -e singular commands: bide, site, lige, hęfe, sciepe, swęre; plurals retain their selected present stems. Hebban/hęfe and licgan/lige require their own consonant alternations.
Weak-II singular command changes -ian to -a; plural retains -iað: lufa/lufiað.
The selected complete weak-III pairs are hafa/habbað, leofa/libbað, saga/sęcgað, hoga/hycgað. Cook also gives sęge for saga and lifiað beside libbað, with optional e in sęcg(e)að/hycg(e)að.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Variants are documented reference alternatives, not automatic extra recall targets; nabban remains unassigned here.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Don has dō/dōð, gan gā/gāð; wesan/bēon gives wes/wesað and bēo/bēoð. No positive willan command pair or modal command pair is invented.
Cook notes shortened plural -e before an immediately following subject pronoun: binde gē, not bindað gē. This positional command variant is distinguished from indicative inversion.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Assigned commands omit the subject or use a preposed subject. No unrestricted plural -e production target, and no first/third-person command system.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: An earlier supplied dictionary citation does not constitute learned infinitive syntax. Only explicitly selected plain-infinitive cells are promoted; exact prior IDs may be retained with old analysis and history preserved.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Four defective modal headwords remain citation labels, with no infinitive/inflected target. Unselected earlier lexical rows get no milestone.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: For selected -an infinitives the course chooses -anne after tō; -ian therefore gives -ianne and geminated stems remain geminated. Contracted final -n gives -nne: fōnne, sēonne, dōnne, gānne, bēonne. The preposition tō is a separate token.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: -enne is a documented valid variant; selected -anne is not a universal grammatical requirement or a license to derive unattested modal cells.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: A finite selected modal/volitional verb takes a plain infinitive in the bounded same-subject construction; the finite verb marks person/number and present/past, while the infinitive does not agree.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: These lexical senses differ. Do not treat every modal as English must, or replace actual indicative past by an automatically hypothetical would/could reading.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Selected cuman + tō + inflected infinitive expresses the purpose of the same subject’s coming. Cook also documents bare infinitives with motion/specification/purpose.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: No claim that all purposes require tō; a valid bare-purpose alternative can miss the stated target without being ungrammatical. General accusative-and-infinitive and dependent-subject syntax remain outside scope.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Ordinary ne before a second-person imperative gives a negative command.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Construction only; the evidence does not teach ondrǣdan, its reflexive/genitive frame, or a nyllan imperative system.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Source-local habban + tō-inflected infinitive describes something held/available for the named action.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Not a general rule translating all habban+tō as modern have to obligation, nor an assigned passive-infinitive system.

productive_outcomes: Use all twelve present/preterite subjunctive person-number cells of each of 56 selected lexical systems, plus the alternative six-cell bēo present series, with their endings, stem changes and exceptions.

Use elementary passives with wesan/bēon and weorðan in statements, commands and wishes; state/result versus event is a tendency, not an absolute distinction.
Use five new complete indicative systems and the complete tōtwǣman command pair, with their separately taught lexical frames.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Adjectivally used participles agree in gender, number and case, with the strong/weak choices already taught for adjectives. Present -ende follows the grēne-type strong declension; it is not a masculine agent noun in -end.

Cook61: present participles in the predicate as nominative/accusative are generally uninflected. Cook62: predicate past participles are generally indeclinable or take strong masculine endings. Cook179 allows uninflected predicate participles. Thus neuterplural dēor bunden is acceptable; dēor bundene is also licensed in verbal passive usage. Do not judge them by an obligatory attributive neuter-u rule.

Heavy-stem disyllabic participles can lose the unstressed vowel before vowel-initial inflections: bundenes→bundnes, bundenum→bundnum; hīeredes→hīerdes, hīeredum→hīerdum, hīerede→hīerde. Full vowels are often restored in West Saxon. Keep the full stem before -ne/-re/-ra; doubled n in bundenne is ordinary. Short-root fręmed/nęred and lufod retain their vowel in the selected model. Rare -u cells above are transparently paradigm-derived.

Weak participles are lexical principal parts, not a universal past-minus-e shortcut: hīerde→hīered, fręmede→fręmed, lufode→lufod, sealde→seald, worhte→worht, sętte→sętt, sęnde→sęnd, lǣdde→lǣd. Before inflection, syncope can bring a dental into contact with a voiceless stem and cause -t-, as Fulk113 scierped→scierpte. These audit examples do not newly assign unlisted verbs.

A past participle of an intransitive verb need not be passive. Source wæs geworden is a become/come-to-pass resultative closure, not a transitive passive. Auxiliary tense does not force one Modern English tense/aspect translation.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Sunu: N/A singular -u, G/D singular -a; N/G/A plural -a, D plural -um. The vowel is short. Cook records variation -u/-o outside genitives and dative plural, and later a-stem sunes/sunas. These are valid documented alternatives, not the selected target or an invitation to assign other u-stem lemmas.

Geðeahtend follows the masculine -end agent-noun pattern, not the inflecting present participle. Selected singular geðeahtend/-es/-e/zero; plural N/A geðeahtend, G geðeahtendra, D geðeahtendum. N/A plural -e and rarer -as are documented alternatives.

Rīce has singular rīce/rīces/rīce/rīce and plural rīcu/rīca/rīcum/rīcu. The lexical -e disappears before the case ending. Cook explicitly allows inserted i/e in the plural after c/g: rīciu/rīcia etc.; these are valid unselected variants.

Use explicit diagnostic stems: angel→angl-, fōdor→fōdr-, but ðyrel retains e. Cræft retains æ before its consonant cluster. Ealdormann follows mann in the final member: dat.sg and N/Apl ealdormęnn. Strong -e nouns replace final e before endings; -nes has -ness-. Smiððe/sīde are weak feminines; fyrspearca/trēowwyrhta/scēowyrhta/wyrhta/cęmpa weak masculines.

Behēfe is an -e adjective: replace lexical e with endings; selected strong feminine nominative singular and neuter N/A plural behēfu. Welig and manig retain medial i in the selected full paradigms and take -u in those cells (weligu/manigu). Wīs is heavy and lacks -u there. Wīsra adds comparative -r- without umlaut and declines weakly; genitive plural wīsra reduces doubled r beside s under Wright §259.3, as earlier lēofra does beside f. Strong feminine N/A plural -e is valid alongside selected -a; other variant cells require their own cited evidence rather than free analogical substitution. Manig is productive only as ordinary plural attributive many; its singular cells are recognition reference, without assigning many-a or substantival/partitive quantity constructions.

Hlæst wares and bęlg bellows are selected as plural; singular counterparts are recognition reference and do not add an unassigned singular sense.
